author: Michael Boyd
title: GameStop ( GME ) continues to be one of the most divisive co
text:
GameStop ( GME ) continues to be one of the most divisive companies out there, and I suspect there will be a lot of “buy the dip” mentality out there as the impact of the weak full year guidance and news of the write-down within Technology Brands sinks in. The problem with that approach is that it simply hasn’t worked in the past with GameStop; buyers that have ended up quickly underwater as results have continued to weaken.
The company has been the quintessential value trap for the better part of two years now, having done an excellent job of luring in both novice retail investors (it screens cheaply) and more hardened model-driven buyers (it looks undervalued under DCF models with steady state expectations).
Both groups have consistently ignored more bearish scenarios, and written off the sky-high short interest. That has been unfortunate, as rather than considering exactly why more than a third of outstanding shares remain shorted – a figure that has not eased as the equity value has collapsed – bulls seem content to ignore the short side story here. “This time is different” and “A short squeeze is just around the corner” are all comments I suspect to see in response to my thoughts.
Technology Brands Looking More Like A Bust Technology Brands was meant to be a strong differentiator, a key diversification move into end markets with greener pastures than the legacy gaming business. Shareholders responded positively at first, and with good reason. Partnerships with AT&T ( T ) and Apple ( AAPL ) brought significant clout at first glance. Further, the company clearly had expertise in real estate management and running a storefront, had strong core competencies within the “buy, sell, trade” dynamic that is common within wireless devices, and there was the opportunity to utilize the existing customer base to drive cross-selling opportunities.
This was a big move, and GameStop has spent plenty of capital developing its Technology Brands segment so far. Total acquisitions have rung the register for nearly $800mm (along with $140mm in capital expenditures). Bolstering these positives, some trends have appeared to be clear tailwinds. For instance, AT&T’s continued advances to diversify from telecommunications into other connected businesses – DirecTV, home security, connected car services, potential Time Warner (NYSE: TWX ) merger – all combine to give GameStop’s Spring Mobile storefront a little more opportunity versus just selling phone plans.
Results haven’t lived up to that hype. And still, despite all the weakness, many bulls could point to the guidance of $82mm in operating earnings (“EBIT”) this year; the business trades at only a touch above a 7-8x EV/EBITDA multiple for the company’s investment. It is not all sunshine and rainbows, however, and the first place I’ll start will be with GameStop guiding for $75mm in EBIT on a 1,000 location store count back during its September 2014 Investor Day:

*GameStop, September 2014 Investor Day 
Growth was, and has been, behind schedule against this blueprint. GameStop did reach that store front target at the end of its fiscal 2016, but segment operating earnings and revenue have never come close to those initial targets in my view. While the company did claim achieving this EBIT target last year – it reported $90mm in adjusted operating earnings - it did so by excluding $20mm in store closure costs, as well as $17mm in property and equipment asset impairments.
Such costs simply shouldn’t be occurring on such recent purchases, and this should have been the first sign that management has been a poor allocator of capital. The $350-400mm in guided asset impairments that will hit this segment this year is yet another example, and as a result, GameStop will, once again, miss the $75mm goal on a GAAP basis. Further, it will take a store count of 1,506 – 50% more than originally anticipated – to hit its profitability target on even an adjusted basis.
Why the issues? There are significant concerns within the operating model here, primarily built upon the Spring Mobile stores and their agreements with AT&T:
Mobile phone growth in the United States is limited from today, and comp store traffic is likely to be low given the high market saturation. Contributing to this, the loss of direct subsidies from carriers on phones has harmed the length of the upgrade cycle. In regards to comp traffic, GameStop does not willingly disclose these numbers in their SEC filings, but management did disclose comp traffic was down 11.5% in Q3 (primarily due to the later iPhone release). The reality is likely low-to-mid single-digit growth on a go-forward basis in the best of times. No advantage to its scale other than incremental benefits from operating leverage. GameStop’s Spring Mobile stores are not given any preferential treatment in procuring inventory versus smaller retailers, in either cost or first rights. This is fundamentally different than the traditional gaming business where GameStop can often procure advantages versus other retailers. Low moat. There are few barriers to entry to becoming an authorized AT&T retailer. Upfront costs are mild, which is why the industry is so fragmented currently. Competition is high. AT&T holds total control. The vast majority of revenue comes in the form of commission income from AT&T based on customer contracts. The fact that AT&T can change this contract at whim (which drove the impairment charge) shows the significantly weak position that GameStop finds itself in. I’ve seen many investors questioning why GameStop did not negotiate a contract firming up its relationship with AT&T as the company deals with the fallout of the reduction in compensation. I’ve reached out to other authorized sellers and the fact is this simply isn’t the norm in this business for anyone. AT&T has the position of power here; the only reason they use authorized resellers is to clamp down on capital investment needs and to outsource the hire of cheap labor, which could bring with it poor public relations fallout.
If margins are highly attractive (or if work is subpar), AT&T is incentivized to do the work themselves, cutting out the middleman altogether. Fact of the matter is GameStop has no strength from a negotiating position. While admittedly Dan DeMatteo is only serving as interim CEO during J. Paul Raine’s absence for medical issues, statements like these do not inspire confidence (from the Q3 2017 conference call):
So, the compensation changes that they took in place reflected investments that they had made and growth there is that are important to them and important to us and differentiate us from the competition and we’ve pushed hard to be a good partner to drive the bundling strategy, which drives greater stickiness of the customer, and we’ve worked hard on that and they’ve recognized that… 
That is a fumble of a run-on response to deal economics, and tells me as a potential shareholder nothing other than to run the other way. What investment has AT&T made?
